title: The Sheep That Destroyed Iceland's Forests
event_summary: When Norse settlers arrived in Iceland beginning around 874 AD, roughly 25-40% of the island was covered in birch forests. Within 60 years, settlers had imported tens of thousands of sheep whose relentless grazing, combined with timber harvesting for longhouses and charcoal production, destroyed nearly every tree on the island. By the time the Althing was established in 930 AD, Iceland had crossed an irreversible ecological threshold — the thin volcanic soils, exposed without root systems, began eroding into the sea at catastrophic rates.
why_forgotten: The Icelandic sagas glorified settlement as a heroic founding narrative, not an ecological catastrophe. The destruction happened gradually across decades, making it invisible as a single 'event.' Additionally, environmental history as a discipline only emerged in the late 20th century, so the collapse was long treated as natural landscape rather than human-caused devastation.
why_it_matters: Iceland's deforestation became one of history's clearest case studies in how colonization triggers irreversible environmental collapse, directly influencing modern soil science and desertification research. The Icelandic Soil Conservation Service, founded in 1907 as the world's first national agency of its kind, was created specifically to address this medieval damage — and its models now guide anti-desertification programs across the Sahel, Central Asia, and beyond. Iceland today remains less than 2% forested, a living monument to how a single imported species can permanently reshape a landmass.
